meta.title: Who really said "There is no talent so ardently supported, nor generously rewarded, as the ability to convince parasites they are victims"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Thomas Sowell, but his 1999 column reads "Few skills are so well rewarded..." The "ardently supported" wording traces to a 1999 Usenet post.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is no talent so ardently supported, nor generously rewarded, as the ability to convince parasites they are victims'?
meta.ogDescription: Sowell's documented line is "Few skills are so well rewarded as the ability to convince parasites that they are victims" (1999). The popular wording isn't in his print.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The thought is Sowell’s, but not these words. His 1999 “Random Thoughts” column reads “Few skills are so well rewarded as the ability to convince parasites that they are victims,” and a 2012 National Review column has “In politics, few talents are as richly rewarded…” The “ardently supported, nor generously rewarded” version is first recorded in a March 1999 Usenet post, and no Sowell text has been found that contains it.

source.heading: What Sowell actually wrote

docMeta.dd: Random Thoughts: Of liberals, parasites and politics
Atlanta Journal, 5 March 1999, p. A14 (syndicated; per Barry Popik)
“Few skills are so well rewarded as the ability to convince parasites that they are victims.”

source.excerpt: In politics, few talents are as richly rewarded as the ability to convince parasites that they are victims. Welfare states on both sides of the Atlantic have discovered that largesse to losers does not reduce their hostility to society, but only increases it.
trail: Barry Popik cites Sowell’s syndicated column “Random Thoughts: Of liberals, parasites and politics” (Atlanta Journal, 5 March 1999, p. A14), which reads “Few skills are so well rewarded as the ability to convince parasites that they are victims.” Barry Popik ↗

Popik’s first record of the “ardently supported, nor generously rewarded” wording is a post to the newsgroup alt.atheism on 21 March 1999, credited to “Tomas Sowell.” He calls it “possibly a misquote,” but thinks it more likely that Sowell repeated the quip on TV or radio in slightly different words. Barry Popik ↗

Sowell used the line again in “Largesse for Losers,” National Review, 10 April 2012: “In politics, few talents are as richly rewarded as the ability to convince parasites that they are victims.” National Review (archived) ↗
Quote Investigator’s two Sowell articles cover other lines, and Wikiquote’s Thomas Sowell page does not list this quotation. Quote Investigator ↗
source.excerptNote: Taken from Sowell’s 10 April 2012 National Review column “Largesse for Losers,” read in an archived copy. The 1999 newspaper version is one sentence: “Few skills are so well rewarded as the ability to convince parasites that they are victims.” Neither text contains the phrase “ardently supported, nor generously rewarded.”

source.rightsNote: Both documented versions are in modern works by a named author: a 1999 syndicated newspaper column and a 2012 National Review column, so both are under copyright in the US. The popular “ardently supported” wording has not been traced to any published Sowell work, so this page cannot name a work it belongs to. It is certainly not public domain.

author.name: Thomas Sowell
author.heading: About Thomas Sowell
author.metaLine: Born 1930 · American economist, economic historian & social theorist
author.bio: Thomas Sowell was born on June 30, 1930, in Gastonia, North Carolina, and grew up in Harlem. He became an economist and a senior fellow at the Hoover Institution. For decades he wrote a widely syndicated newspaper column, including recurring Random Thoughts pieces made of one-line observations. That format is why so many short, punchy lines get credited to him. He received the National Humanities Medal in 2002.

The “ardently supported, nor generously rewarded” wording appears in neither.

misattribution.heading: Where the polished wording came from
misattribution.intro: Sowell did write this idea. What has drifted is the wording. The version on most memes reads more smoothly than anything found in his columns, and the earliest place it has been found is an online post, not his own text.

items.why: In Barry Popik’s chronology, “There is no talent so ardently supported, nor generously rewarded, as the ability to convince parasites they are victims” first appears in a newsgroup post credited to “Tomas Sowell,” later that same month, after the 5 March 1999 column. Popik suggests Sowell may have said it this way on air, but cites no broadcast. Barry Popik ↗

items.who: Twitter/X posts and quote images, 2008 onward
items.why: Popik records the “ardently supported” version on Twitter on 7 November 2008. A Thomas Sowell quotes account posted the column wording (“Few skills are so well rewarded…”) in 2010, 2017 and 2022, and the 2012 “In politics…” wording in 2016. So all three versions circulate side by side. Barry Popik ↗

misattribution.truthLine: What Sowell printed: “Few skills are so well rewarded as the ability to convince parasites that they are victims” (Atlanta Journal, 5 March 1999). He reused it as “In politics, few talents are as richly rewarded as the ability to convince parasites that they are victims” (National Review, 10 April 2012 ↗).

context.heading: A one-liner from a column of one-liners
lead: Sowell regularly filled a column with short, unconnected observations under the heading “Random thoughts.” Jewish World Review’s archive of his columns lists several in 1999 alone (JWR Sowell archive ↗). Lines from columns like these are easy to lift and reword, and they are the kind of lines that end up as quote images.

When Sowell came back to the parasites line in 2012, he followed it with a claim about welfare states: “largesse to losers does not reduce their hostility to society, but only increases it.” Quote images drop that context. They also usually swap in the smoother “ardently supported, nor generously rewarded” wording, which has not been found in anything Sowell published.
